title: Who Actually Manages?
author: Uwe Mierisch
summary: Uwe Mierisch argues that management is an activity rather than a title or a group of bosses. He notes that phrases like "Management has decided" or "Management just won't decide" let everyone off the hook: bosses get a title and everyone else gets someone to blame. Citing Peter Drucker in 1967, he says any knowledge worker whose contribution materially affects results is an executive. He illustrates with an engineer preparing a test, who must create the preconditions (rig, parts, technician, software), measure progress to see where to step in, and adjust early. A department head or top executive does the same thing at a larger scope. If people leave management to the bosses, the engineer waits, problems go unnoticed, and the boss is asked to manage what he cannot see. His closing point is that delegating management upward means giving away your own work.
points: Mierisch defines management as an activity everyone performs inside their own area of responsibility, not as a group of people at the top.
His working formula is to create the preconditions for execution, measure to spot where action is needed, and adjust early.
The same activity scales from an engineer to a department head to top management; only the scope changes.
Treating management as someone else's job produces waiting, late discovery of problems, and bosses managing things they cannot see.
The practical challenge is to ask in your own team who actually manages, and to stop delegating that work upward.
quotes: It just isn’t true. Management isn’t a group of people. Management is something you do.
Peter Drucker saw this back in 1967. For him, every knowledge worker responsible for a contribution that materially affects the results was an executive, whether or not anyone reported to him.
He measures. Not to write a report, but to see where he needs to step in. Measuring is how you spot where action is needed.
Create the preconditions, measure, adjust. All within his own area of responsibility.
Then the engineer waits until someone books the test rig. Nobody notices a missing part until the test is due.
In the way we talk, management is a group. If you’re a boss, you’re in it. Everyone else isn’t.
If you delegate management upward, you give away your own work.
